Student protests erupt at Cornell over mishandling of gang-rape allegations

Protests erupted at Cornell University on Monday as students criticized officials for their handling of gang-rape allegations, demanding the president’s resignation and painting “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” on an administrative building. The demonstrations were sparked by a high-profile case involving a former student, known as Jane Doe, who alleged she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. Protesters called for the banning of fraternities and criticized the university for failing to protect students. The vandalism at Day Hall, the building housing the president’s office, included messages like “AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED PROTESTORS ARE EXPELLED.” The university condemned the vandalism, stating it was not the answer to expressing concerns.

The case has drawn international attention, with critics accusing Cornell of being too lenient with the accused men and failing the victim. According to lawyers for Jane Doe, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the incident, while others faced suspensions or required to write reflection papers. The university has faced backlash for its handling of the case, with students and faculty demanding stronger action against sexual violence on campus.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that four student demonstrators were suspended in 2024, while CBS News and The New York Post do not mention any suspensions. The Guardian attributes the painted messages to students protesting the treatment of pro-Palestine protesters, while FOX News and The Daily Wire do not mention this context. The Daily Wire claims Jane Doe consented to the sexual activity and later retroactively claimed she was assaulted, a claim not mentioned in other accounts. The New York Post and The Guardian describe the alleged incident as a gang rape, while CBS News and The Daily Wire do not specify the nature of the alleged assault beyond the presence of ketamine.

Sources The Guardian · CBS News · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Straight Arrow News · New York Post

US death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say

Christa Pike, a 50-year-old death row inmate in Tennessee, survived a failed execution attempt last week, according to her lawyers. She was administered two doses of pentobarbital, a barbiturate used in lethal injections, but did not die. Pike, who was convicted in 1996 for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, remains in critical condition in a Nashville hospital, intubated and on a ventilator. Her lawyers reported that she is "conscious and speaking" and has suffered "severe damage" to her arms. The Tennessee Department of Correction has halted all executions in the state and ordered an independent investigation following the botched attempt.

Pike’s legal team had previously warned that her medical history, including a blood-clotting condition and small veins, made lethal injection a risky and potentially painful method. They had sought alternative execution methods, such as hanging or a firing squad, but the Supreme Court overruled a stay of execution. The failed attempt has raised questions about the reliability and humanity of lethal injection as a method of execution.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that Pike is "conscious and speaking" and that experts and her legal team say her recovery is "unprecedented." Mother Jones states that Pike "remains intubated, on a ventilator" and that her arms are "swollen, burned and blistered." The Nation says Pike "has not spoken since the failed execution." These accounts differ on Pike’s current state of consciousness and physical condition.

Sources BBC · Mother Jones · The Daily Wire · The Dispatch · Slate · The Nation

Supreme Court Begins New Term With Major Cases On Immigration, Gun Rights, Climate Lawsuits

The Supreme Court opened its new term Monday with a series of high-profile cases that include challenges to President Trump’s immigration policies, gun control measures, and climate-related lawsuits. The justices are also facing political pressure as Trump criticizes his appointees and Democrats consider changes to the Court. The term includes cases on Arizona’s voter registration requirements, the legality of deporting migrants to third countries, and the constitutionality of AR-15 bans. The Court also began its term with a major climate case, Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, where Boulder, Colorado, seeks to hold energy companies liable for climate damages.

The Court’s emergency docket has become increasingly important as the justices consider urgent issues related to elections and immigration. The administration’s immigration policies face two major tests, with the Court set to hear cases on mandatory detention for certain immigrants and the legality of deporting migrants to countries where they are not citizens. The Court has allowed deportations to continue while the litigation proceeds. The term also includes a case on the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style weapons and a climate case that could affect dozens of similar lawsuits nationwide.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and Axios both mention the Court’s consideration of Arizona’s voter registration requirements and the administration’s immigration policies, but only Axios explicitly states that the Court allowed the administration to restart third-country deportations. The Daily Wire does not mention this specific action. The Daily Caller and Slate provide more detailed accounts of the climate case, including the arguments and the involvement of specific justices, while FOX News and The Daily Wire focus more on the broader implications and legal arguments without the same level of detail on the case specifics.

Sources The Daily Wire · Axios · FOX News · The Daily Caller · Slate · NPR

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Three Years After October 7, Survivors and Analysts Reflect on the Attacks and Their Aftermath

The third anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel has prompted renewed reflection on the event and its consequences. Survivors like Keith Siegel, who was held hostage for 484 days, describe the trauma of the attacks and the ongoing struggle to rebuild. The attacks resulted in the deaths of 1,209 people, including 36 children, and the abduction of 251 individuals, with 47 killed and 76 taken to Gaza in the kibbutz of Nir Oz. The event has also sparked debates about Israel’s military response and the broader regional implications. Analysts, including those from The Washington Examiner, have discussed the long-term strategic impact on Israel and the Middle East, noting the country’s military successes against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran. Meanwhile, other outlets have focused on the human toll, the political fallout, and the international context of the conflict.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner reports on the decline in nontraditional sexual identity among young Americans, citing a drop in "LGB" identification among high schoolers and a decline in bisexual, transgender, and queer identifications among students aged 14-25. The Guardian focuses on the personal trauma of survivors, including Keith Siegel’s experience as a hostage and the broader impact on the kibbutz of Nir Oz. The Free Press highlights the memoir of Avinatan Or, a Hamas hostage, detailing his captivity and survival. The Daily Wire provides an analysis of Hamas’s founding charter, emphasizing its religious motivations and framing the conflict as a religious struggle. NPR reports on new revelations that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was warned about the potential Hamas attack, while Al Jazeera focuses on the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, detailing the devastation and ongoing suffering of the population.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · The Free Press · The Daily Wire · NPR · Al Jazeera

Hasan Piker says 9/11 remark ‘far less damaging’ than Trump’s ‘take out’ LA and San Diego

Hasan Piker, a left-wing Twitch streamer and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, compared his 2019 remark that America "deserved" 9/11 to President Donald Trump’s comments suggesting Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego. Piker claimed his remark was not nearly as harmful as Trump’s. Trump made the remarks during a campaign rally in Nebraska, defending the war with Iran and suggesting the conflict was a "small price to pay" for safety. The comments drew swift condemnation from California officials, including Governor Gavin Newsom, who called them "deranged and dangerous." The White House later attempted to clarify that Trump was not suggesting Iran should attack U.S. cities, but rather that the U.S. was fighting to prevent Iran from doing so.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and Newsweek both report that Piker claimed his 2019 remark was less damaging than Trump’s comments. The Washington Examiner adds that Piker speculated Democrats would not go after Trump for his remarks, while Newsweek notes that Piker apologized for the remark, clarifying it was about U.S. foreign policy, not the victims of 9/11. The Guardian and CBS News do not mention Piker’s comparison or apology. The ABC News and Newsweek accounts differ in that Newsweek states the White House defended Trump, while ABC News reports that the White House’s Rapid Response account denied Trump’s remarks were suggesting Iran should attack U.S. cities.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · ABC News · CBS News · Newsweek · BBC

U.S. officials monitor suspected plague case in Russia after researcher dies

A Russian lab technician died after contracting pneumonia, prompting U.S. officials to closely monitor the situation. The Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk is under scrutiny as the cause of death remains unclear. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated the administration is watching the situation but emphasized there is no cause for alarm. The U.S. government is assessing options and has its most serious travel warning in place for Russia due to the war with Ukraine. The incident has raised concerns about global biological threats and the need for pandemic preparedness. Russian authorities have placed nearly 200 people under medical observation and quarantined several hospitals following the death. The Russian health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said no microorganisms linked to the woman's work were found in her biological samples. The World Health Organization (WHO) was informed that no plague or other high-threat pathogen was detected among her close contacts, though confirmation is pending.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that the cause of death is "pneumonia of undetermined etiology" and that there are conflicting accounts of how the researcher got sick. It also mentions the possibility of a genetically altered strain of plague and the need for more information to determine the appropriate response. BBC states that the cause of death was "pneumonia of undetermined etiology" and that no microorganisms linked to her work were found in her biological samples. It also notes that the Russian health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, found no emergency situation at the institute. Straight Arrow News provides more specific details about the deceased, Daria Shipilova, and mentions that she broke a test tube containing the pathogen. New York Post and FOX News both mention the possibility of a bioweapon and antibiotic resistance, with FOX News citing a former senior Trump official warning that the case could be "far worse" than the plague. Washington Examiner focuses on Trump's planned call with Putin and the U.S. government's willingness to help Russia contain any possible outbreak.

Sources Axios · BBC · Straight Arrow News · New York Post · Washington Examiner · FOX News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Disgraced Former House Speaker Dead At 84

Dennis Hastert, the longest-serving Republican House Speaker, has died at 84, according to a local coroner. He died at his home over the weekend. Hastert, who served as House Speaker from 1999 to 2007, was known for his role in shaping President George W. Bush’s legislative agenda. He later admitted to sexually abusing boys during his time as a high school wrestling coach and was sentenced to prison for financial crimes related to hush money payments. He was released from federal prison in 2017.

Hastert was born in 1942 and worked as a teacher and wrestling coach at Yorkville High School before entering politics. He was elected to the Illinois House of Representatives and then to the U.S. House in 1986. He became House Speaker after Newt Gingrich stepped down in 1998 and Bob Livingston resigned due to extramarital affairs. He led the House until Republicans lost their majority in 2006. After resigning from Congress in 2007, he worked as a lobbyist until his indictment in 2015 for financial crimes.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and CBS News both state that Hastert was the highest-ranking elected U.S. official to serve a prison sentence, while FOX News and Straight Arrow News do not mention this claim. The Daily Wire and CBS News attribute the claim about the prison sentence to the U.S. attorney, Zachary Fardon, while FOX News and Straight Arrow News do not attribute the claim to any specific source. ABC News and Axios do not mention the claim about being the highest-ranking official to serve prison time.

Sources The Daily Wire · FOX News · ABC News · CBS News · Axios · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford

The US military removed its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, England, following a threat to the base, according to President Donald Trump. The Pentagon confirmed the bombers, thought to be about a dozen, were moved back to their home stations in the US. Trump stated the decision was made due to intelligence suggesting a threat, though he did not specify its nature. The move came after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the airbase. The exact nature of the threat remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated it might have involved sabotage or an attack on the bombers in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran.

The incident at RAF Fairford led to the arrest of five men and a sixth British-Iranian national, all released on bail. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested there were "strong indications" Iran was involved, while Iran denied any role. The US still maintains the ability to strike Iran with its remaining forces in the Middle East. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the movement of the bombers as a routine rotation, while Vice President JD Vance linked the decision to an "abundance of caution" against Iran.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that Trump refused to be drawn on the nature of the threat, while ABC News states Trump said "we know who made the threat" but did not confirm the identity. Straight Arrow News claims the withdrawal was connected to existing threat reporting, not a new threat, whereas The New York Post and The Daily Wire describe the move as a response to new intelligence about an Iran-backed plot. The Guardian does not specify the nature of the threat or the exact number of bombers moved, while The Daily Wire mentions that some aircraft left while aerial refueling was still in progress.

Sources BBC · ABC News · Straight Arrow News · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: A former CIA official defrauded taxpayers of $200 million by faking classified programs, directly impacting millions through lost public funds.

Ex-US spy who stashed gold bars in his home admits to $200m scam

A former CIA officer, David Rush, 49, pleaded guilty to wire fraud after admitting to defrauding the US government of nearly $200 million. Prosecutors stated that Rush created fake classified programs to justify the acquisition of luxury real estate, gold bars, and other assets. During an FBI raid in May, agents found 298 gold bars, $2 million in cash, and 35 luxury watches at his home. Rush also confessed to providing top secret data to a foreign government official, which could have endangered a clandestine human source.

Rush admitted to fabricating a "Special Access Program" to justify expenditures, including the purchase of four Florida properties and luxury vehicles. Court filings indicate he used fraudulent public funds to acquire these assets and directed wire transfers totaling $145 million. Prosecutors said he used the funds to buy real estate, which he intended to resell for profit. The plea deal requires Rush to forfeit the gold bars, cash, real estate, vehicles, and watches, as well as pay restitution to the government.

Where the accounts differ

BBC and The Daily Wire both report that Rush admitted to providing top secret data to a foreign government official, while Just The News and FOX News attribute the disclosure of the clandestine human source to Rush. The Daily Wire and CBS News mention the $194 million figure, while BBC and FOX News cite $200 million. The Washington Examiner and CBS News do not specify the exact amount of the fraud, only that it was nearly $200 million. The Daily Wire and CBS News mention the $45 million wire transfer, while BBC and FOX News refer to it as part of the $200 million scheme. The Daily Wire and CBS News also note that Rush lied about his education and military background, while BBC and FOX News do not mention this detail.

Sources BBC · The Daily Wire · Washington Examiner · CBS News · FOX News · Just The News

Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad - a first for US military since World War Two

The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first such military execution in more than 60 years. Nidal Malik Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it. The execution will mark the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two. Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan. The attack on 5 November 2009 was the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines. Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row. A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.

Where the accounts differ

BBC states the execution will be the first since the end of World War Two, while The Hill says it will be the first since 1961. The Guardian and Newsweek do not specify the exact year of the last military execution by firing squad. Just The News and FOX News both mention 1961 as the last military execution by firing squad. The Guardian and Newsweek differ in the number of casualties, with the Guardian stating 12 soldiers and 30 wounded, while Newsweek says 13 dead and more than 30 wounded. FOX News attributes the claim that Hasan said "I shot to kill" to a Sanity Board report, while the other accounts do not mention this. The Guardian and Newsweek provide more detail about Hasan's background and mental state, while FOX News includes information about Hasan's alleged visit to a strip club and his actions during the attack.

Sources BBC · Just The News · The Guardian · Newsweek · The Hill · FOX News

Christa Pike survived failed execution attempt in Tennessee

Christa Pike, a convicted murderer, was scheduled for lethal injection in Tennessee on September 30, 2026. The execution was halted by a federal court stay just before it began, leading to a nine-hour wait at the prison. After the stay was lifted, Pike was taken to the death chamber, where she was administered two doses of pentobarbital. She remained conscious for part of the process, breathing heavily and snoring, before being taken to a hospital. Her lawyer, Stephen Ferrell, stated she remains critically ill and unconscious, with an unclear prognosis. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year following the botched attempt.

Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate. Her lawyers had previously warned that her medical condition, including a platelet disorder and small veins, made lethal injection a risky and potentially painful method. The state had previously botched an execution attempt in May 2026 with Tony Carruthers, leading to a suspension of executions. The Department of Correction's communications director, Dorinda Carter, announced the execution was proceeding after the stay was lifted.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that the execution was halted by a federal court stay and that the process took place in the death chamber with witnesses present. BBC and The Nation describe Pike as remaining unconscious and critically ill, with her lawyer stating the prognosis is unclear. The Nation adds that Pike's lawyers had warned about the risks of lethal injection due to her medical history. Straight Arrow News mentions that prison officials followed a protocol requiring a second dose if the first failed, leading to life-saving measures. Washington Examiner and New York Post note that Pike may not fully recover and that her condition remains critical. The Nation also highlights the broader context of botched executions in Tennessee and the state's history of failed attempts.

Sources NPR · BBC · Washington Examiner · New York Post · The Nation · Straight Arrow News

Jim Bakker, famed televangelist felled by scandal, dies at age 86

Jim Bakker, the televangelist who built a Christian broadcasting empire before it collapsed in scandal, has died at the age of 86. His second wife, Lori Bakker, announced his death on social media, stating he "went home to be with the Lord." Bakker and his first wife, Tammy Faye Bakker, became one of television's most recognized couples with their PTL show, which preached to millions of viewers that Christian faith and financial success were compatible. Their success led to the launch of an amusement park-like community in North Carolina. Bakker's world came crashing down in 1987 when he admitted to a sexual relationship with a secretary named Jessica Hahn, who accused him of abuse. A year later, he was indicted on federal financial charges and spent five years in prison. Bakker returned to television ministry and married Lori.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that Bakker was sentenced to 45 years in prison but the sentence was later reduced, while Newsweek states he was sentenced to 45 years and later received a reduced sentence of eight years. The Guardian and ABC News mention that Bakker was convicted of defrauding followers of $158 million, while Newsweek states the amount was $158 million. The Guardian and The Guardian also note that Bakker was defrocked after the sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, while Newsweek attributes this to Bakker's own statement that he was "set up" by former colleagues. The Guardian and The Guardian also mention that Bakker was defrocked after the sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, while Newsweek attributes this to Bakker's own statement that he was "set up" by former colleagues.

Sources Just The News · The Guardian · NPR · ABC News · CBS News · Newsweek

Obama to campaign with fellow Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in key Michigan Senate race

Former President Barack Obama will campaign alongside Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit on October 24, according to multiple outlets. The event will also feature Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who is running for governor. The Senate race is considered one of the most competitive in the midterm cycle, with the outcome potentially determining control of the Senate. Obama has been selective in his campaign appearances since leaving office but has increased his public presence in the final stretch of high-stakes elections.

Obama’s involvement in the race follows a pattern of increased participation in recent midterms, including appearances in Detroit during the 2022 and 2024 elections. He has also recorded a series of campaign ads for Democratic candidates, which will be released in the coming weeks. The event is expected to draw large crowds and prominent guests, with some outlets noting that Obama’s presence could provide a significant boost to El-Sayed’s campaign, particularly in Detroit, where he remains highly popular.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Daily Wire report that El-Sayed’s campaign has faced scrutiny over past statements, including a resurfaced video clip where he criticized Mackinac Island. The Daily Wire attributes this to El-Sayed, while The Guardian does not mention the clip. The Guardian also notes that El-Sayed has made opposition to US military aid to Israel and criticism of its conduct in Gaza central to his campaign, a detail absent in other accounts. The Nation highlights that El-Sayed’s opponent, Mike Rogers, falsely claimed he had pledged support to the Muslim Brotherhood and said “America deserved 9/11,” which The Daily Wire attributes to Rogers, while The Guardian does not mention these claims.

Sources Just The News · ABC News · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · The Nation

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor launches legal action against police over Epstein raids

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is challenging the legality of search warrants that led to police raids on his homes in February 2026. The legal action, which includes a judicial review, is being heard in a private high court hearing before Mr Justice Hilliard. The warrants were issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court and allowed police to search his Sandringham estate residence and his former home, Royal Lodge. Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, following the release of documents from the U.S. Justice Department’s Epstein investigation. The arrest occurred on his 66th birthday, and he was released under investigation after being questioned for several hours. The legal challenge is part of a broader dispute over the validity of the warrants and the evidence obtained during the searches.

Thames Valley Police confirmed they are involved in legal proceedings related to the warrants but declined to comment further. The police investigation into misconduct in public office continues, with allegations that Mountbatten-Windsor shared sensitive information with Epstein during his tenure as the UK’s trade envoy. The legal action marks the first time a member of the royal family has challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Hill both mention that Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on his 66th birthday, while The Daily Caller and NPR state the arrest occurred on the day of his 66th birthday. The Guardian and The Hill note that the arrest was linked to the Epstein files, while The Daily Caller and The Hill also mention the specific allegations of sharing sensitive information with Epstein. The Guardian and The Hill report that the arrest was the first time a senior British royal was placed under arrest in nearly 400 years, while The Daily Caller and The Hill state it was the first time in nearly four centuries. The Guardian and The Hill attribute the claim about the first royal arrest in nearly four centuries to The Telegraph, while The Daily Caller and The Hill do not attribute this claim to a specific source.

Sources The Guardian · Newsweek · BBC · The Hill · NPR · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Mass shootings leave two people dead in Georgia and 12-year-old girl dead in Baltimore, sparking community trauma and renewed calls for gun reform.

Mass shootings leave two people dead in Georgia and 12-year-old girl dead in Baltimore

A mass shooting in Vienna, Georgia, resulted in two deaths and at least 25 injuries, according to authorities. The incident occurred at a homecoming block party with over 1,000 attendees, where shots were fired at about 50 people in two locations just after 1 a.m. on Sunday. The victims killed were not immediately identified, though the Georgia Bureau of Investigation later named them as Ja’Quavion Aderious Jackson, 21, and Macaleb Malik Jackson, 23. The shooting in Baltimore left a 12-year-old girl dead and three others wounded after gunfire broke out over a parking spot near a youth football event at Leon Day Park. The police commissioner described the incident as an argument between two individuals who opened fire on each other, with the girl being a bystander hit by gunfire.

The 12-year-old girl was pronounced dead at the scene, and a 25-year-old woman with her was also shot. Two men, aged 23 and 28, were wounded but not believed to have life-threatening injuries. The Baltimore mayor condemned the incident as one of the most disgusting events he had seen, highlighting the girl’s presence at a youth football event.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the Georgia shooting occurred at a gathering of more than 1,000 people and that the two victims killed were not immediately identified. It also mentions that the 12-year-old girl was a bystander at a nearby field and that the shooting in Baltimore was linked to a youth football event. Newsweek identifies the two victims killed in Georgia as Ja’Quavion Aderious Jackson and Macaleb Malik Jackson and states that the shooting left 35 injured. FOX News also names the victims as Jaquevion Jackson and Macaleb Jackson but notes that the shooting was not at a school-sponsored event, a claim not made by the other outlets. The Guardian and Newsweek both mention the 12-year-old girl was a bystander, while FOX News does not specify her location relative to the shooting.

Sources The Guardian · Newsweek · FOX News

Brazil heads to a runoff election after Bolsonaro and Lula fail to garner a majority of votes

Brazil’s presidential election resulted in neither candidate securing a majority, leading to a runoff between incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The electoral court confirmed that both candidates will face off in a second round on October 25. Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, while Bolsonaro, 45, is running as the leading right-wing candidate. The election comes amid a polarized political climate, with significant implications for Brazil’s future direction and its relationships with global powers.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and Al Jazeera both state that Bolsonaro received 47% of valid votes and Lula 45.1%, while the Guardian reports Bolsonaro with 47% and Lula with 45.1%. The Guardian also mentions Bolsonaro received 56.1 million votes to Lula’s 53.8 million, a figure not included in the Washington Examiner or Al Jazeera. The BBC and Newsweek do not provide specific vote counts but note that neither candidate reached the 50% threshold. The Guardian and Al Jazeera mention Bolsonaro’s lead over Lula in the first round, while the BBC and Newsweek describe the race as closely contested with polls showing them roughly tied. The Guardian and Al Jazeera also note that Bolsonaro’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup, a detail included in the BBC and Newsweek but not in the Guardian or Al Jazeera.

Sources Washington Examiner · BBC · The Guardian · NPR · Al Jazeera · Newsweek

Trump praises Israeli hero who thwarted cockpit attack, calls him 'my plumber'

President Donald Trump praised Israeli citizen Yaniv Hayoun, a Flydubai passenger who helped subdue a radicalized Omani co-pilot during a mid-flight attack, calling him “my plumber” and a “Trump fan.” Trump shared a video on his Truth Social account highlighting Hayoun’s actions, which he described as heroic. The incident occurred on a FlyDubai flight from the UAE to Tel Aviv, where the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the pilot and attempted to take control of the aircraft. Passengers, including Hayoun, intervened to stop the attack, with Hayoun entering the cockpit to subdue the attacker. The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

The incident has also drawn attention to security concerns at the RAF Fairford air base in the UK, where five British nationals were arrested on suspicion of planning a terror attack. The U.S. removed its bombers from the base following the arrests, citing security concerns. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated there were “strong indications” that Iran was involved, though Iran denied any role. The U.S. and UK are collaborating on the investigation, with the UK emphasizing the complexity of the case.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and The Guardian both report that the co-pilot was an Omani national named Hammam al-Hammami, who had studied engineering at RMIT University in Australia and left before completing his degree. The Guardian adds that al-Hammami was barred from flying by Oman over extremist concerns and was later hired by Flydubai. The New York Post does not mention al-Hammami’s name or his educational background. CBS News and The Washington Examiner do not mention the co-pilot’s name or his ties to Australia, focusing instead on the UK arrests and U.S. security concerns. FOX News and The Daily Wire refer to the co-pilot as an Omani national but do not name him or mention his Australian ties.

Sources New York Post · CBS News · Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Guardian

US Coast Guard searches for missing air ambulance off coast of Massachusetts

The US Coast Guard confirmed it found debris from a medical transport aircraft off the shore of Massachusetts’ Nantucket Island and is searching for the six people who were on board. The jet lost contact with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) during a flight from Bermuda to Boston on Saturday morning. The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers onboard when it departed Bermuda’s LF Wade International Airport overnight for the flight to Massachusetts. The plane was flying at 24,000 feet (7,300 metres) for much of the journey before descending 13,000 feet in about two minutes shortly before flight controllers lost contact. The Massachusetts Port Authority confirmed the aircraft did not arrive at Boston Logan International Airport as scheduled.

The FAA issued a search-and-rescue alert notice for the Gulfstream G-100 at about 1.20am local time Saturday. The plane is operated by Latitude Air Ambulance, based in Ontario, Canada, and provides medical evacuation services. The company’s website states it has run thousands of missions since 2009 with a "flawless safety record." The Coast Guard deployed two search and rescue planes, a helicopter, and a motor lifeboat to continue the search. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is gathering information but has not provided an update on the situation.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both state the plane departed Bermuda at 12:41am on Saturday, while FOX News and Straight Arrow News report the departure time as 11:41pm on Friday. The Guardian and CBS News mention the plane descended 13,000 feet in about two minutes, while FOX News and Al Jazeera report the plane plummeted from 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in three minutes. The Guardian and CBS News attribute the statement about the plane descending to flight data, while FOX News and Al Jazeera attribute it to FlightAware data. The Guardian and CBS News note the FAA issued a search-and-rescue alert at 1:20am, while FOX News and Straight Arrow News report the FAA issued the alert at 1:20am as well, but Al Jazeera states the FAA alerted the Coast Guard at about 2am on Saturday. The Guardian and CBS News mention the plane had four crew members and two passengers, while FOX News and Al Jazeera specify the composition as two Canadian pilots, two medical staff, a patient, and a relative.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · CBS News · FOX News · Al Jazeera · Straight Arrow News

Trump names national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new AI czar

President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will serve as the White House AI czar. Clayton will lead a new initiative called the "Super Intelligence Force," which Trump claims will ensure the United States remains a global leader in the development of artificial intelligence. The force will coordinate federal engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and technology companies.

Clayton, who previously served as the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York and chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, has called super intelligence a "national security issue." He has also pushed back against calls for a "pause" in AI development, arguing that other countries are continuing to advance the technology. The White House announced that Clayton will lead a three-month effort to assess the "risks and opportunities" of AI, with a report due within 120 days.

Where the accounts differ

NPR states that Clayton called super intelligence a "national security issue" and that Trump's "Super Intelligence Force" will "coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies." FOX News reports that Trump said the force will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," and that it will report directly to him and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. CBS News adds that the force will include Andrew Ferguson, Emil Michael, and Scott Kupor as members, and that Clayton will report to Trump and Wiles. The Guardian notes that Trump created an "AI Force" and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for "bad" development, and that Trump met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns. Straight Arrow News mentions that the force will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Washington Examiner does not mention the composition of the force or the role of other officials.

Sources Washington Examiner · NPR · FOX News · CBS News · Straight Arrow News · The Guardian

Attorney for accused Cornell student calls on Letitia James to step aside over prior comments

An attorney for one of seven former Cornell University fraternity members accused in a civil lawsuit has raised concerns about New York Attorney General Letitia James’ impartiality in the criminal investigation. Andrew Miltenberg, representing one of the accused, argued that James’ earlier public statements supporting the accuser created an appearance of bias. The case involves allegations that seven fraternity brothers drugged and sexually assaulted a female student at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some claiming the sexual activity was consensual and others denying participation. No criminal charges have been filed against the seven men.

Cornell University’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, expressed deep sorrow over the case, calling it one of the most challenging periods for the university. He pledged greater transparency amid mounting outrage over how the school handled the case. The woman, identified as Jane Doe in court documents, alleges she was sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024 and has sued the university and seven former students. The case has also renewed scrutiny of the “voluntary intoxication loophole” in New York law, which makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving victims who voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and the New York Post differ on the number of men involved in the alleged rape. The Washington Examiner states that Giuffra believes more men were involved than the seven listed in the lawsuit, while the New York Post does not mention any discrepancy in the number of accused individuals. The New York Post also attributes the claim about James’ bias to Rensselaer County Executive Steven McLaughlin, while the Washington Examiner does not name a source for the claim about James’ impartiality. The FOX News account provides more detail on Miltenberg’s objection, including his statement that James’ earlier comments created an “avoidable question about the appearance of impartiality,” which is not explicitly stated in the Washington Examiner or the New York Post.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · NPR · New York Post · FOX News · Al Jazeera

No source labeled left covered this story.

Japan Issues 'Strong Protest' After US Marine Accused of Killing Woman

A U.S. Marine has been arrested in connection with the death of a woman in Okinawa, prompting the Japanese government to lodge a protest with the United States. The incident occurred in Naha, Okinawa’s capital, where the suspect, identified as Devin J. Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal with the Third Marine Expeditionary Force, was found by police. Japanese authorities allege that Ballard robbed and killed Anna Yagi, 39, who was found dead at a hotel in Naha. Ballard has denied the allegations. The Japanese government has called the incident "extremely brutal and heinous" and demanded strict discipline and preventive measures from the U.S. military. The U.S. embassy in Tokyo has stated it is cooperating with Japanese authorities in the investigation.

The U.S. military maintains a significant presence in Japan, with around 55,000 personnel stationed across the country, including a substantial number in Okinawa. The incident has raised concerns about the U.S. military presence in the region, particularly given the history of crimes involving U.S. service members in Okinawa. Japanese officials have emphasized the need for maximum cooperation with the investigation and stricter measures to prevent future incidents.

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek and The Guardian both report that the suspect is identified as Devin J. Ballard, while ABC News and Straight Arrow News refer to him as Devin Jacob Ballard. The Guardian and NPR mention that the suspect is a 20-year-old Marine, while Straight Arrow News states he was arrested around 1 a.m. local time. ABC News and BBC report that the cause of death was suffocation due to pressure on the neck, while The Guardian and NPR do not specify the cause of death. The Guardian and NPR also note that the suspect was arrested after being spotted in an entertainment district, while Newsweek and Straight Arrow News do not mention this detail. The Guardian and NPR provide additional context about the history of crimes involving U.S. military personnel in Okinawa, which is omitted in Newsweek and Straight Arrow News.

Sources Newsweek · ABC News · The Guardian · NPR · BBC · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

California Realtor Accused of Spying for China on Taiwan President’s Son

A 34-year-old California realtor, Wanying “Heather” Zhang, was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday as she attempted to depart for China. Federal authorities allege she acted as an unregistered agent of the People’s Republic of China, surveilling a close relative of a Taiwanese government official. The FBI and U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli stated that Zhang coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection, failing to notify the Attorney General of her foreign government activities, which is a federal offense. The FBI’s Rapid Response account confirmed the arrest, and the case includes alleged text exchanges and surveillance activities in Seattle, Washington.

Zhang is accused of traveling to Seattle in 2025 to surveil the son of Taiwan’s president, Lai Ching-te, and sending photos, videos, and license plate information to Chinese officials. The FBI alleges she used a rented car to photograph the family’s residence and shared the data with handlers. The Justice Department claims her activities date back to September 2022, with communications involving two individuals believed to be Chinese government officials. The case is part of a broader context of heightened tensions between China and Taiwan, with the U.S. maintaining a strong stance in support of Taiwan’s sovereignty.

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek and The Guardian both state that the FBI did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target but shared a report from the New York Post identifying him as Lai Ting-yu. However, the New York Post and Al Jazeera explicitly name Lai Ting-yu as the target, while Newsweek and The Guardian do not. The New York Post and FOX News describe specific text exchanges between Zhang and a Chinese government official, including a message where Zhang allegedly identified the target as “that young one.” This detail is absent in Newsweek and The Guardian. Additionally, the New York Post and FOX News mention that Zhang and her associate rented a black Nissan Rogue and used a neighbor’s security camera to capture their actions, which is not included in the accounts from Newsweek, The Guardian, or Al Jazeera.

Sources Newsweek · New York Post · FOX News · The Guardian · Just The News · Al Jazeera

White House Monitors Suspected Plague Case in Russia

The White House is monitoring reports of a suspected plague case in Russia, according to a Trump administration official. A 28-year-old woman, Daria Shipilova, worked at an anti-plague research institute in Irkutsk, Russia, and died after breaking a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen. She was hospitalized on Sept. 29 with severe pneumonia and died between Oct. 1 and 2. Russian authorities imposed quarantines at several medical facilities and placed nearly 200 people under medical observation. Russian health authorities have not confirmed that Shipilova contracted plague, stating she had "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that tests found no microorganisms linked to her work. The White House referred questions to the State Department, which did not respond to a request for comment.

Russian officials have taken precautionary measures in response to Shipilova's death, including quarantining hospitals and monitoring contacts. The Russian public health agency described the epidemiological situation in the region as stable. Some outlets reported that five hospitals were placed under quarantine, while others cited three. The number of quarantined hospitals and the exact number of people under observation vary across reports.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones reports that five hospitals were quarantined, while The Daily Caller and Straight Arrow News mention three. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller state that 200 people were placed under quarantine, while Axios and Straight Arrow News report nearly 200. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller claim that Shipilova broke a test tube containing live Yersinia pestis, a claim not explicitly made by Axios or Straight Arrow News. The Daily Caller and The Daily Wire mention that some Russian officials cast doubt on the test tube incident, while Axios and Straight Arrow News do not. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller attribute the claim about the test tube to The Moscow Times, while Axios and Straight Arrow News do not specify the source.

Sources Axios · Mother Jones · The Daily Wire · FOX News · The Daily Caller · Straight Arrow News

The brief ends here.

Ex-US Attorney will lead independent review of Christa Pike botched execution

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee appointed former US attorney Ed Stanton to lead an independent investigation into the botched execution of death row inmate Christa Pike. The review follows the failed attempt to execute Pike on Wednesday, during which she received two doses of pentobarbital and survived. Pike, who was convicted of murdering her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, remains unconscious and intubated in a Nashville hospital. The state halted all executions in Tennessee for nearly three years after the botched attempt, including the case of Oscar Smith, and resumed executions in February 2025 with a new single-dose protocol. Commissioner Frank Strada resigned after the failed execution, calling the review “entirely appropriate and necessary.”

The new lethal injection protocol, introduced by Strada, uses a single dose of pentobarbital instead of a three-drug cocktail. This change was prompted by a 2022 investigation into Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol, which found that drugs used in prior executions were not being tested properly. Pike’s attorneys claim she experienced intense pain during the injection and developed blisters and burns around the injection site, suggesting the IV may not have been properly connected. The state’s execution team reportedly used at least seven needles in Pike’s left arm during the attempt to establish an IV line.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and The Hill both report that Pike’s attorneys claim she experienced intense pain and developed blisters and burns around the injection site, suggesting the IV may not have been properly connected. The Washington Examiner and Axios do not mention these specific details. The Federalist and BBC do not discuss the medical details of Pike’s condition or the IV complications. The New York Post and The Hill attribute the claim about the IV complications to Pike’s attorneys, while the Washington Examiner and Axios do not specify who made the claim. The BBC provides more context about the victim, Colleen Slemmer, and includes quotes from a journalist who has covered many executions, while the other accounts do not mention this.

Sources New York Post · BBC · Washington Examiner · The Federalist · Axios · The Hill

Brazil's election pits Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro

Brazilians are voting in a presidential election on Sunday, with Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva, the left-wing incumbent, facing Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth term, while Bolsonaro, 45, is running as the standard-bearer of his father's political movement. Jair Bolsonaro, who served as president from 2019 to 2023, is currently serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election. The election will determine whether Brazil continues under Lula's left-leaning government or returns to the Bolsonaro movement. Polls suggest a tight race, with both candidates hovering around 40% in the latest surveys, and a runoff likely if neither secures more than 50% of the vote.

The election has broader implications, particularly for U.S. influence in Latin America. The Trump administration has imposed tariffs on Brazilian goods, sanctioned a Supreme Court justice, and designated Brazil's two largest gangs as terrorist organizations. A Bolsonaro victory could align Brazil more closely with U.S. policies, including a hardline approach to crime and a focus on securing critical minerals. Lula, meanwhile, has emphasized Brazil's sovereignty and criticized the U.S.-led "war on drugs" for its impact on the Amazon and Brazil's democratic institutions.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that Flávio Bolsonaro used an AI-generated image of his father to endorse his candidacy, while The Daily Caller notes that Flávio met with Trump at the White House in May and pledged Brazil would join Trump's "Shield of the Americas" initiative if he wins. Newsweek and Axios both mention the U.S. sanctions on Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, but Newsweek adds that Trump ordered 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July 2025, while Axios states the tariffs were imposed in the summer of 2026. The Guardian and NPR both describe the election as a rematch of the 2022 contest, but The Guardian adds that Trump has been actively promoting right-wing candidates in Latin America, while NPR highlights the potential impact on Brazil's Supreme Court and environmental policy.

Sources BBC · Newsweek · The Guardian · NPR · Axios · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Coast Guard finds debris from medical plane carrying 6 people

The U.S. Coast Guard confirmed finding debris off Nantucket, Massachusetts, from a medical transport plane that disappeared while flying from Bermuda to Boston. The plane, a Gulfstream G100, was carrying four Canadian and two Bermudian nationals. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) reported losing contact with the aircraft early Saturday, prompting a search. The Coast Guard deployed search and rescue assets, including planes and a helicopter, to locate the missing aircraft and any potential survivors.

The plane, operated by Latitude Air Ambulance, was en route to Boston Logan International Airport when it vanished. Flight data indicates the aircraft dropped rapidly in altitude before losing communication. An air traffic controller asked the pilot, "You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" and later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency. Emergency crews were warned to prepare for the plane's arrival due to reported electrical issues and loss of radio and radar.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and The Guardian both state the plane dropped at least 9,000 feet over two minutes before leveling off, while FOX News and CBS News report the plane plummeted from 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in three minutes. The Guardian and CBS News mention the plane was set to land at Boston Logan International Airport at 1:30 a.m., while NPR and The Daily Wire do not specify a landing time. FOX News and The Guardian attribute the altitude drop to FlightAware data, while CBS News and BBC cite FlightAware as well. The Daily Wire and BBC mention the plane was flying at 24,000 feet before descending 13,000 feet in about two minutes. The Guardian and CBS News note the FAA issued a Search and Rescue Alert Notice at about 1:20 a.m., while NPR and The Daily Wire report the FAA alerted the Coast Guard at roughly 2 a.m. and 1 a.m., respectively.

Sources NPR · FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · CBS News · BBC

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump, Cotton tussle over daylight savings after cell phone number leak

President Trump repeatedly criticized Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) over his stance on a daylight savings bill after posting the Republican Congress member’s cell phone number on social media. In a morning Truth Social post, the president encouraged his supporters to call the senator and urge him to back legislation that would make daylight savings time the permanent standard time. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act of 2025 in July with broad bipartisan support, but the bill is stalled in the Senate. Trump accused Cotton of holding up the legislation and urged Arkansas voters to call the senator, citing the need for bipartisan support and the benefits of permanent daylight savings time.

Cotton responded with a statement on social media, reiterating his opposition to the bill. He argued that Congress has enacted permanent daylight savings time before but repealed it due to the negative effects of late sunrises in the winter. He emphasized that Arkansans do not want their children to go to school in the dark and that he would always put Arkansas first.

Where the accounts differ

THE HILL reports that Trump claimed the bill would decrease the national crime rate because “CRIMINALS DON’T LIKE WORKING IN THE LIGHT,” a claim not included in other accounts. FOX News states that Trump argued the bill would “decrease Robbery and Murder Rates, Reduce Car Accidents (especially those involving Pedestrians!), Lower Risk for Cardiac Issues, Stroke, and Seasonal Depression,” a more detailed list of benefits not found in THE HILL or CBS News. THE DAILY WIRE mentions that Trump cited a letter from PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp in his post, a detail not included in THE HILL or CBS News. THE GUARDIAN notes that Trump was asked why he posted Cotton’s phone number and responded about the disruption of changing clocks, a detail not included in THE HILL or CBS News.

Sources The Hill · FOX News · The Daily Wire · CBS News · The Guardian · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

French Students Protests Escalate Into Violence Across Schools

French high school students have escalated their protests over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, and deteriorating school facilities into violent clashes with police and rioters. The unrest, which began in working-class areas near Paris, has spread to major cities across France, with reports of schools being set on fire and students using Molotov cocktails. Over 1,000 schools were affected by the protests, with more than 500 high schools shut down or disrupted. The violence has led to arrests, injuries to both students and staff, and government officials blaming the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party for inciting the unrest.

The protests, initially sparked by student grievances over poor educational conditions, have grown into widespread riots. Students have blocked school entrances, set buildings on fire, and engaged in violent confrontations with law enforcement. The government has accused the LFI of orchestrating the violence, while student leaders and teachers unions have called for better funding and resources for schools. The situation has drawn national attention, with political figures and media outlets debating the causes and consequences of the unrest.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that over 560 high schools were completely shut down or disrupted, with more than 160 forced to lock their doors entirely. It also states that 2,000 agitators were arrested, with 90% being minors, and that 65 school staff and 170 students were injured. The Nation, however, mentions that nearly 2,000 people were arrested, with scores of schools closed by administrative order, but does not specify the number of injured. The BBC notes that the LFI is accused of inciting the protests, while the Nation attributes the spread of the movement to a combination of student anger and political factors. The Straight Arrow News states that more than 400 schools were closed Friday, while The Daily Wire reports over 500. The NPR account mentions 5,000 arrests, a figure not included in other reports. The FOX News account states that 2,000 people were arrested, aligning with The Daily Wire and the BBC, but differs in the number of injured and damaged schools.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Nation · BBC · Straight Arrow News · NPR · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump announces $90 checks for 20 million seniors to help cover Medicare premiums

President Trump announced Friday that over 20 million Medicare Part B enrollees will receive one-time payments of $90 to help cover their premiums. The White House fact sheet clarifies that the payment will be $90 per person, with most recipients receiving the money via direct deposit in early October. The funds are sourced from the Medicare Improvement Fund, which Trump labeled a "Slush Fund" used by Democrats to increase healthcare costs. The standard Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90, meaning the $90 payment will offset less than half of the monthly cost. Trump also mentioned that the Medicare Improvement Fund was established in 2008 for improvements to original Medicare’s fee-for-service program.

The administration stated that the payment is separate from other refund initiatives, including $500 checks for over 950,000 Americans who were allegedly overcharged for Obamacare. Trump emphasized that the Medicare checks are part of his effort to protect and preserve Medicare and Social Security, which he claims were on the verge of ruin under President Biden. He also reiterated his promise of a $5,000 "Trump Dividend" for all Americans if Republicans win the midterms.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports the payment is $90, while Fox Business and Newsweek also mention $90, but Fox Business adds that Trump claims the funds come from a "Slush Fund" used by Democrats to pay for "Waste, Fraud, and Abuse for their Special Interest friends." Newsweek attributes the same characterization to Democrats. The New York Post also mentions the "Slush Fund" label but does not specify which party it attributes to. Axios notes that the $90 payment offsets less than half of the monthly premium, a detail also included in Newsweek. Fox Business and the New York Post mention the $5,000 "Trump Dividend" as a separate promise, while Axios and Newsweek reference it as well. The New York Post and Fox Business include Trump's claim that the Medicare Improvement Fund was used by Democrats to raise healthcare costs, which Axios and Newsweek attribute to Trump.

Sources Axios · Fox Business · Newsweek · New York Post

No source labeled left covered this story.

Trump defends data centers in Ohio, warns they’ll go to China if blocked

President Donald Trump addressed a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, on Saturday, urging Republican voters to turn out for midterm elections. He defended the expansion of data centers, claiming they are essential to maintaining U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence and warning that blocking them would allow China to gain an advantage. Trump told the crowd, “There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China.” He also encouraged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot” and to “turn out for a midterm victory.”

Trump highlighted his administration’s efforts to ensure data centers benefit local communities and praised Republican Senator Jon Husted for his legislative efforts to address concerns about rising electricity costs. Husted introduced a bill aimed at shifting costs from consumers to large power users, but it was blocked by Senate Democrats. Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown criticized Husted for providing tax breaks to Big Tech to attract data centers to Ohio, which he now says are making Ohioans pay the price.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that Trump claimed there would be a “big surprise” in the upcoming elections, while the New York Post and The Hill do not mention this claim. The Washington Examiner focuses on Jon Gruden’s presence at the rally and does not detail Trump’s remarks on data centers or the midterm elections. The New York Post and The Hill both mention Trump’s warning about data centers going to China, but the New York Post adds that Trump tied the issue to the global race for artificial intelligence, calling it “superintelligence,” which is not included in The Hill’s account. Al Jazeera and The Hill both attribute the claim about Husted giving tax breaks to Big Tech to Sherrod Brown, while the New York Post attributes it to Brown’s X post.

Sources Al Jazeera · New York Post · The Hill · Washington Examiner · FOX News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Feds charge shop clerk, son with selling illegal kratom after 2 Ole Miss deaths

Federal authorities have charged a store clerk and his son with selling an illegal kratom product following the deaths of two University of Mississippi students. Prosecutors stated that both deaths appear consistent with drug overdoses, though it remains unclear if kratom contributed. The investigation is ongoing, with toxicology reports still pending. One student, Aidan Hamilton, made multiple purchases from a vape, tobacco, and beer store in Oxford, Mississippi, according to court documents. An informant purchased kratom-based pills from the clerk, Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, who warned the informant about the risks. Both Mosleh and his son, Islam Yahya Mosleh, face one count of possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance. The DEA has banned three kratom-related compounds, one of which was found in products linked to the students.

The store where the kratom was sold is under investigation, with federal agents seizing kratom products from the location. The owner of the gas station, Ibrahim Aydah, denied that the pills found near one of the students came from his store, citing differences in packaging and ingredients. He claimed the pills found near the student had a price label and contained different ingredients than those he sells. The DEA confirmed that products listing "pseudoindoxyl" are banned under federal law.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and The Guardian both report that the kratom pills found near the students were labeled "Smax" and that the DEA banned three kratom-related compounds, one of which was found in products linked to the students. FOX News states that the pills found near Robert Strang were labeled "Smax Pseudo-DHM" and lists pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15(DHM) as ingredients, while CBS and The Guardian do not mention these specific ingredients. CBS and The Guardian also note that the students were found in different locations, one on campus and one off campus, while FOX News does not specify the locations of the students' bodies. Additionally, FOX News reports that the owner of the gas station, Ibrahim Aydah, denied the pills came from his store, a claim not made by CBS or The Guardian.

Sources CBS News · FOX News · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Mass protests in Spain over housing crisis highlight systemic eviction threats endangering thousands' homes and livelihoods.

Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87

An 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was evicted from her Madrid apartment in September 2026 after failing to pay a rent increase. The incident sparked widespread protests across Spain, with demonstrators demanding an end to evictions, lower rents, and stronger tenant protections. The government introduced two decree-laws in response, but both were rejected by Congress. The rejection has intensified pressure on Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call a snap election before his term ends in 2027. Protesters have occupied central squares in Madrid and other cities, with some calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.

The protests have drawn attention to the broader issue of rising housing costs in Spain, with many residents struggling to afford rent. Some demonstrators argue that the government’s proposed measures are insufficient, while others believe the crisis has been exacerbated by policies favoring landlords. The eviction of Abascal, who had lived in her apartment since 1956, became a symbol of the housing struggles faced by many Spaniards, particularly the elderly and low-income families.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that 70,000 people protested, while the Guardian also states that organizers claimed 500,000 attended. The BBC reports that the Tenants’ Union claimed 500,000 protesters, while authorities put the number at 70,000. The Christian Science Monitor does not specify a number but notes that “over a thousand people are now camped in Madrid’s most central square.” The Guardian and BBC both mention that the government introduced two decree-laws, but the Christian Science Monitor refers to them as “measures” without specifying they were decree-laws. The Guardian and BBC attribute the rejection of the first decree to a vote of 178 to 172, while the Christian Science Monitor does not specify the vote count.

Sources Christian Science Monitor · The Guardian · BBC

No source labeled lean-left or lean-right or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.
